extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and general readers interested in scholarly peer review and scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing quality criteria, variants, failures, and reform proposals for scholarly peer review systems (pre- and post-publication). Useful for people assessing peer review models, reform proposals, or designing review policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of scientific peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific peer review has been defined as the evaluation of research findings for competence, significance, and originality by qualified experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peers act as sentinels on the road of scientific discovery; the goal is to improve relevance and accuracy of scientific discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review (formal, megajournal model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication review as a formal review method used by megajournals (e.g., Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, F1000Research, Qeios, ScienceOpen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At these journals reviewers are formally invited much like pre-publication journals; articles that pass peer review are included in external scholarly databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal/social-media-based peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of social media and blogs as a means of informal, post-publication peer review where broader scientific community members voice skepticism and critique (example: #arseniclife/GFAJ-1 controversy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactive online communication technologies enable a variety of audiences to observe an informal process of post-publication peer review and can legitimize or delegitimate scientific information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-blind (results-blind) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers receive an edited version of the submitted paper which omits the results and conclusion section so journal acceptance is based on rationale and methods rather than observed outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants include a two-stage version where a second round of reviews or editorial judgment uses the full paper; intended to counteract positivity/publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion-blind review
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors submit a positive and a negative version of the paper; only after acceptance do authors reveal which version is real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed to further reduce bias toward positive results by preventing reviewers/editors from being influenced by outcomes during initial evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered reports / pre-accepted articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals review and accept or reject study protocols (theoretical justification, experimental design, statistical analysis) before data collection or before results are revealed; accepted protocols guarantee publication regardless of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts emphasis from results to research questions and methods; evidence cited shows higher adherence to preregistered plans (e.g., ~92% adherence for registered reports vs ~60% for unreviewed preregistrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended peer review (broader expertise inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Including people and groups with experience beyond working academics in the quality-assurance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If conducted systematically, this can lead to more reliable or applicable results than peer review conducted purely by academics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based assessment of peer review effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality-assurance role of peer review should be supported by empirical evidence; some systematic reviews (e.g., Cochrane) found little empirical evidence that peer review ensures quality in biomedical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for evidence-based peer review and assessment of interventions designed to improve the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and suppression risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review may be biased against provincial authors, those from low- and middle-income countries, early-career researchers, novel or controversial ideas, and can reflect gender and political biases, prestige bias, and homophily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These biases can discourage innovative projects and lead to conformity in funded and published work; simulations and studies indicate such systemic tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and transparency (open peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous, pre-publication peer review may lack accountability and enable abuse by reviewers; open peer review makes comments and often reviewer identities visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open peer review can increase transparency and accountability; examples include F1000, eLife, BMJ, and BioMed Central. However, transparency trade-offs exist (e.g., reviewer candor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest management
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review must address undeclared conflicts of interest and industry-funded research which may corrupt literature; traditional peer review often fails to appropriately address these COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blinded review can reduce some biases but may make COI detection less likely; journals and COPE issue guidance on fraudulent practices and COI handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud detection limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is not designed to detect fraud in raw data and may occasionally detect but generally cannot be relied upon to find fabricated or manipulated data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fraudulent or irreproducible data are published, retraction is a typical remedy, but peer review's structure limits its fraud-detection capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism detection capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers, who see full manuscripts and are familiar with the literature, are better placed to detect textual plagiarism than fabricated data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-plagiarism (autoplagiarism) may be less likely detected in double-blinded reviews; plagiarism remains a known failure mode of the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload, heterogeneity, and scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers differ substantially in the time and effort they invest; there is a growing shortage of scholars willing to review, producing inconsistent review quality and noisy outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heterogeneity among referees can produce arbitrariness in outcomes; recruitment and recognition of peer reviewers remain ongoing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and exploitation concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Most academic publishers do not financially compensate reviewers, leading to criticisms of exploitation of unpaid labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some platforms and publishers have begun paying reviewers or making payment part of the business model; economic feasibility and impact on quality are debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access and peer review quality perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue OA journals might use less formal peer review practices and therefore could publish lower-quality work; studies show OA journals indexed in major databases are approaching similar scientific impact as subscription journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation-based impact studies suggest no inherent reason to avoid OA on quality grounds, particularly in biomedicine and APC-funded journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure handling and retraction procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: When peer review fails to catch fundamental errors or fraud, journals may retract papers, but many have limited procedures beyond publishing letters to the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust post-publication correction workflows and transparent handling of failures are necessary to maintain literature integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake peer review and process-manipulation defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented cases exist where reviewers were faked (authors recommending fake contact details) or rogue editor networks enabled substandard publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers, editorial boards, and COPE issue statements and take steps (retractions, investigations) to mitigate and respond to such fraud; vigilance in editorial checks is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ghostwriting and authorship integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ghostwriting—companies drafting articles later published under academics' names—can corrupt the literature and is difficult for peer review to detect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undeclared industry involvement and ghostwritten contents have led to political/regulatory misuse; stronger disclosure and editorial scrutiny are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of gatekeeping vs culture of doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Gatekeeping by journals confers credibility but may diminish a ‘culture of doubt’; removing or redesigning filtering could restore skepticism but risks populating literature with low-quality or biased content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals include author-controlled review and other alternatives intended to rebalance credibility and skepticism; consequences must be carefully considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered reports' empirical benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered reports have been found to increase adherence to preregistered plans and reduce 'fishing', focusing reviewers and authors on theoretical backing, statistical power, and implications of null results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (analysis of ~100 preregistered studies) suggests higher adherence and potential quality improvements when initial study plans are accepted prior to data collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot evidence on result-blind implementations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilot experiments (e.g., JAMA Internal Medicine’s two-stage result-blind peer review) indicate implementation nuances: unblinded steps may benefit positive studies more than negatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical pilots are necessary to understand how result-blind models affect outcomes and whether they reduce biases as intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recognition and symbolic valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers perform valuable but often invisible work; symbolic recognition (e.g., monuments, public acknowledgment) highlights social value and the need for better recognition systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition may help address recruitment and retention issues, improving voluntary participation and review quality.
